intro.en: Comprehensive clinical template for taking and presenting a paediatric case history and physical examination.

items.summary: Systematic collection of baseline demographic details for a paediatric patient, including legal identity, chronological age, address, and informant reliability.

blocks.title: Core demographic details
bullets: Full name of the child and hospital registration number to prevent misidentification.
Exact date of birth and verified chronological age in completed days, months, or years.
Sex of the child, recorded accurately for gender-specific growth charts and clinical risk profiling.
Residential address and contact details, essential for tracing contacts and mapping endemic illnesses.

blocks.title: Informant details and reliability
bullets: Identity of primary caregiver or informant accompanying the child, usually mother or father.
Assessment of informant reliability based on daily involvement in childcare and consistency of recall.
Language barriers or need for a medical interpreter during clinical interview.
Date and exact time of admission, alongside the precise date and time of clinical examination.

blocks.title: Clinical significance
bullets: Age dictates normal physiological vitals, developmental expectations, and illness vulnerabilities.
Exact chronological age is critical for calculating precise fluid volumes and drug dosages.
Informant reliability caveats must be documented early to frame diagnostic certainty.

viva.q: Why is recording exact age more critical in paediatrics than in adult medicine?
viva.a: Paediatric vital signs, developmental milestones, fluid requirements, and drug dosages vary strictly with age. Even small errors in age alter interpretation of growth percentiles and medication safety.

viva.q: How do you assess and document informant reliability during history taking?
viva.a: Reliability is judged by whether the informant lives with the child, provides consistent chronological details, and directly observes symptoms. Discrepancies or secondary informants are explicitly noted in the case record.

image.brief: A clean paediatric clinical case sheet showing structured demographic entry boxes for child name, date of birth, sex, caregiver relation, and reliability score.

items.summary: Sequential listing of the primary symptoms prompting presentation, recorded chronologically from earliest to most recent with precise durations in caregiver words.

blocks.title: Rules of recording chief complaints
bullets: Arrange complaints in strict chronological order from the earliest symptom to the most recent.
Use non-technical terminology reflecting the caregiver description rather than medical jargon.
Record the exact duration of each presenting complaint in hours, days, weeks, or months.
Limit the list to three or four primary symptoms directly related to the acute illness.

blocks.title: Common presentation patterns
bullets: Fever with duration, documentation of pattern, and associated chills or rigors.
Cough, noisy breathing, or respiratory distress with time of onset.
Diarrhoea, vomiting, poor feeding, or lethargy in infants.
Seizures, altered sensorium, or abnormal movements with precise timing.

viva.q: Why must chief complaints always be recorded in chronological sequence?
viva.a: Chronological listing reconstructs the natural progression of illness, highlights which organ system was initially affected, and helps distinguish primary disease from secondary complications.

viva.q: What terminology should a candidate use when writing chief complaints?
viva.a: Candidates should use plain descriptive terms provided by the informant, such as loose stools or rapid breathing, rather than interpretive diagnostic labels like gastroenteritis or pneumonia.

image.brief: Clinical documentation layout displaying a bulleted list of presenting symptoms aligned chronologically with adjacent duration brackets.

items.summary: Comprehensive chronological elaboration of each presenting symptom, exploring onset, progression, variations, associated features, negative history, and baseline physiological functions.

blocks.title: Symptom elaboration framework
bullets: Mode of onset: sudden, acute, or insidious progression from the state of health.
Progression: whether symptoms are worsening, improving, static, or occurring in discrete episodes.
Aggravating and relieving factors, including changes with feeding, posture, or medications.
Temporal and environmental variation: diurnal fluctuations, seasonal patterns, or postural changes.
Pain characterisation using SOCRATES: site, onset, character, radiation, association, timing, exacerbating factors, severity.

blocks.title: Pertinent negative history
bullets: Systematic inquiry to exclude specific differential diagnoses relevant to the complaints.
Screening for red flag signs such as convulsions, inability to feed, cyanosis, and lethargy.
Documenting absence of features indicating multi-organ involvement or systemic toxicity.

blocks.title: Baseline functions and pre-morbid health
bullets: Pre-morbid growth trajectory and activity level of the child prior to acute deterioration.
Current bowel habits: frequency, consistency, presence of blood, mucus, or change from normal.
Current bladder habits: frequency of wet nappies, urine output, dysuria, crying during micturition.

viva.q: What is the clinical value of eliciting negative history in paediatric HOPI?
viva.a: Pertinent negatives actively rule out competing differential diagnoses, identify absence of severe complications or red flags, and narrow the diagnostic possibilities before physical examination.

viva.q: How does assessing bowel and bladder habits contribute to HOPI evaluation?
viva.a: Urine output is an immediate indicator of hydration and renal perfusion, while stool changes reveal gastrointestinal loss, systemic infection, or dysentery.

image.brief: Mind-map diagram illustrating paediatric HOPI breakdown into symptom progression, diurnal variation, pertinent negatives, and pre-morbid growth.

items.summary: Detailed account of outpatient or inpatient interventions received prior to referral, ongoing investigations, and current supportive or therapeutic medications.

blocks.title: Outside treatment details
bullets: Medical consultations prior to index admission, noting outpatient or inpatient management.
Specific medications administered: antibiotics, antipyretics, steroids, or bronchodilators.
Dosage, route, timing of last dose, and compliance or duration of completed drug courses.
Response to previous therapy, including clinical improvement, failure, or adverse reactions.

blocks.title: Investigations and in-hospital management
bullets: Diagnostic tests performed: blood counts, blood cultures, sputum testing, lumbar puncture, or radiography.
Status of test results: reviewed reports versus pending or unknown laboratory investigations.
Current supportive interventions: intravenous fluid type and infusion rate, oxygen therapy.
Current scheduled medications: oral drugs, intravenous antimicrobials, and anticonvulsants.

viva.q: Why is prior antibiotic administration significant when evaluating a febrile child?
viva.a: Prior antibiotics can partially treat bacterial meningitis or sepsis, sterilising blood or cerebrospinal fluid cultures while altering typical clinical and laboratory manifestations without eradicating the infection.

viva.q: What details regarding outside treatment must be elicited from the caregiver?
viva.a: Document the setting of care, exact drug names, doses, duration, route, response to treatment, whether investigations like lumbar puncture were performed, and any observed adverse drug reactions.

image.brief: Flowchart tracing pre-referral outpatient care, outside laboratory tests, current intravenous infusions, and ongoing inpatient medications.

items.summary: Record of previous childhood illnesses, exanthemata, chronic diseases, prior hospitalizations, surgical interventions, and known drug or environmental allergies.

blocks.title: Infectious and chronic paediatric illnesses
bullets: Specific inquiry for childhood exanthematous infections: measles and chickenpox (varicella).
History of recurrent wheezing or diagnosed bronchial asthma.
History of contact with or treatment for pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis.
Prior episodes sharing clinical features with the current presenting illness.

blocks.title: Hospital admissions, surgery, and allergies
bullets: Details of previous hospital admissions: age at admission, reason, duration, and discharge diagnosis.
Past surgical operations or invasive procedures, including anaesthetic complications.
Known adverse drug reactions, cutaneous drug eruptions, or anaphylaxis.
Food allergies, atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, or environmental hypersensitivities.

viva.q: Why is past history of measles specifically asked in paediatric history?
viva.a: Measles causes profound immune suppression predisposing to severe pneumonia, tuberculosis activation, chronic diarrhoea, and late complications such as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

viva.q: How does a history of recurrent similar complaints alter clinical formulation?
viva.a: Recurrent episodes indicate underlying chronic pathology, structural anomalies, immunodeficiency, or atopy rather than an isolated, self-limiting acute infectious illness.

image.brief: Checklist diagram displaying past childhood medical illnesses including measles, varicella, asthma, tuberculosis contact, surgeries, and drug allergies.

title.en: Antenatal, natal, and neonatal birth history

items.summary: Comprehensive chronological evaluation of intrauterine course across all three trimesters, delivery events, resuscitation, and neonatal period health.

blocks.title: Antenatal history by trimester
bullets: First trimester: febrile illness with rash (TORCH screen), exposure to teratogenic drugs, radiation, severe hyperemesis.
Second trimester: maternal quickening perception, gestational diabetes screening, blood pressure monitoring, anomaly ultrasound.
Third trimester: gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, antepartum haemorrhage, fetal movements, maternal infections.

blocks.title: Natal history and delivery events
bullets: Gestational maturity at delivery: preterm (<37 weeks), term (37-41 weeks), or post-term.
Place and mode of delivery: institutional or home, spontaneous vaginal, assisted, or caesarean section.
Immediate birth status: whether the baby cried immediately or required active bag-mask resuscitation.
Birth weight in kilograms and gestational age classification: AGA, SGA, or LGA.
Timing of first breastfeed initiation, ideally within one hour of birth.

blocks.title: Neonatal transitional period
bullets: Duration of nursery or postnatal ward stay with the mother.
History of significant neonatal jaundice, onset within 24 hours, need for phototherapy or exchange transfusion.
Neonatal respiratory distress, grunting, chest indrawing, or cyanosis requiring oxygen.
Admission to Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) or NICU with duration and interventions.
Early neonatal feeding practices, including colostrum administration and prelacteal feeds.

viva.q: Why is delayed crying at birth significant for long-term paediatric outcomes?
viva.a: Delayed crying indicates birth asphyxia and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, which can lead to cerebral palsy, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and developmental delay.

viva.q: What maternal conditions in the first trimester pose the highest fetal risk?
viva.a: First-trimester maternal febrile exanthems like rubella, teratogenic medications, radiation exposure, and uncontrolled diabetes lead to organ dysgenesis, congenital heart defects, and microcephaly.

image.brief: Three-stage timeline diagram detailing trimester-specific antenatal maternal health, labour and delivery milestones, and neonatal transitional events.

items.summary: Systematic inquiry into milestone acquisition across gross motor, fine motor, personal-social, language, visual, and auditory developmental domains.

blocks.title: Key functional domains
bullets: Gross motor development: head control, rolling, unsupported sitting, standing, walking, and running.
Fine motor and adaptive skills: grasping patterns, hand regard, bidextrous to pincer grasp, scribbling, block building.
Personal and social milestones: smiling, maternal recognition, stranger anxiety, waving, toilet independence.
Language and communication: vocalisation stages from cooing and babbling to single words and sentences.
Sensory competence: visual fixation, tracking, binocular coordination, and auditory orientation to sound.

blocks.title: Developmental assessment principles
bullets: Compare attained functional age with chronological age to calculate developmental quotient.
Differentiate isolated domain delay from global developmental delay involving two or more streams.
Screen for developmental regression where previously acquired milestones are lost.

viva.q: How do you distinguish global developmental delay from isolated speech delay?
viva.a: Global delay entails significant delay across two or more core developmental domains, whereas isolated speech delay preserves normal gross motor, fine motor, and personal-social milestone trajectories.

viva.q: What is the clinical definition and significance of milestone regression?
viva.a: Regression is the active loss of previously established developmental skills, signalling neurodegenerative disorders, progressive metabolic encephalopathies, or refractory epileptic encephalopathies.

image.brief: Radar chart illustrating the four developmental streams: gross motor, fine motor adaptive, personal-social, and language communication.

items.summary: Quantitative and qualitative assessment of food intake using 24-hour recall, evaluating dietary pattern, allergen exposure, total calorie-protein intake, and nutritional deficits.

blocks.title: Qualitative dietary habits
bullets: Dietary classification: lacto-vegetarian, ovo-vegetarian, or mixed omnivorous diet.
History of food intolerances, milk protein allergy, or adverse reactions to specific foodstuffs.
Feeding practices: breastfeeding duration, bottle feeding, dilution of animal milk, hygiene practices.

blocks.title: Quantitative dietary calculation
bullets: Perform a detailed 24-hour dietary recall measuring all foods and liquids consumed using standard measures.
Calculate total daily energy intake in kilocalories and compare with expected caloric requirements.
Calculate total daily protein intake in grams and compare with age-specific recommendations.
Express nutritional adequacy as percentage deficit in calories and deficit in proteins.

viva.q: How do you calculate dietary caloric deficit in a paediatric patient?
viva.a: Sum the caloric value of all foods in the 24-hour recall, compare against the child's expected daily calorie requirement for age or weight, and calculate the difference as a percentage deficit.

viva.q: Why is diluted milk consumption hazardous in young infants?
viva.a: Over-dilution reduces caloric and protein density, causing severe undernutrition, while contaminated water introduces enteric pathogens causing recurrent infective diarrhoea and growth faltering.

image.brief: Diagram depicting a 24-hour dietary intake record with calculation columns for food quantity, calories, protein content, and calculated percentage deficit.

items.summary: Systematic audit of vaccination status according to national guidelines, inspection of BCG scar, and documentation of recent, due, and optional vaccines.

blocks.title: Routine immunisation audit
bullets: Inspect left deltoid or forearm for physical presence of a healed BCG scar.
Verify receipt of birth doses: BCG, oral polio vaccine (OPV-0), and Hepatitis B birth dose.
Audit primary infant series: pentavalent or hexavalent, rotavirus, pneumococcal, and inactivated polio vaccine.
Review measles-containing vaccines (MR or MMR) administered at 9 and 15 months.

blocks.title: Current status and optional vaccines
bullets: Document exact date and type of the most recent vaccine received by the child.
Identify scheduled vaccines that are currently due or overdue for chronological age.
Inquire regarding optional or non-national schedule vaccines (influenza, varicella, Hepatitis A, typhoid).
Record any history of severe post-immunisation adverse events, anaphylaxis, or prolonged crying.

viva.q: What does the absence of a BCG scar imply in a vaccinated child?
viva.a: Absence of a scar does not necessarily indicate lack of immunity; approximately 10 to 15 percent of successfully vaccinated infants do not develop a visible scar. Repeat vaccination is not routinely advised.

viva.q: How do you classify a child whose vaccines are behind schedule?
viva.a: The child is documented as partially immunised, and an age-appropriate catch-up immunisation schedule is formulated without restarting completed primary doses.

image.brief: Immunisation audit grid tracking infant vaccines, booster timing, BCG scar verification, and overdue vaccine alerting.

items.summary: Construction of a three-generation pedigree chart, documentation of parental consanguinity, and screening for hereditary, infectious, and allergic diseases.

blocks.title: Pedigree construction and structure
bullets: Construct a standard three-generation pedigree chart with index case (proband) clearly indicated.
Record parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, and uncles with health status and ages.
Document pregnancy losses, stillbirths, spontaneous abortions, and unexplained early sibling deaths.
Specifically document presence and degree of parental consanguinity (first-cousin, uncle-niece).

blocks.title: Familial and environmental disease screening
bullets: History of close contact with active pulmonary tuberculosis or chronic coughing family members.
Familial predisposition to non-communicable disorders: diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease.
History of atopic diathesis in family: asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema.
Inherited haematological and metabolic disorders: thalassaemia, haemophilia, or neurometabolic disease.

viva.q: Why is eliciting consanguinity critical in paediatric neurology and genetics?
viva.a: Consanguineous unions significantly increase the risk of homozygous expression of rare autosomal recessive conditions, such as metabolic storage diseases, spinal muscular atrophy, and congenital malformations.

viva.q: What symbols are used to denote males, females, and affected individuals in a pedigree?
viva.a: Males are represented by squares, females by circles, deceased members with diagonal strike-through lines, and affected individuals by fully shaded symbols, with an arrow designating the proband.

image.brief: Pedigree chart displaying three generations with standard genealogical symbols: squares for males, circles for females, double lines for consanguinity, and an arrow for proband.

items.summary: Standardised assessment of household socio-economic status using the Modified Kuppuswamy scale alongside environmental sanitation and living conditions.

blocks.title: Modified Kuppuswamy classification
bullets: Evaluates three parameters: education of the head of household, occupation, and family monthly income.
Scores categorise families into five strata: Class I (Upper), II (Upper middle), III (Lower middle), IV (Upper lower), V (Lower).
Monetary income slabs must be updated periodically against consumer price index adjustments.
Guides understanding of resource limitations, food security, and treatment affordability.

blocks.title: Living environment and sanitation
bullets: Type of housing: pucca (concrete), semi-pucca, or katcha (mud and thatch) dwelling.
Overcrowding index: number of occupants per room, ventilation, and indoor kitchen smoke exposure.
Source of drinking water: treated municipal piped supply, tube-well, or unprotected surface water.
Sanitation facilities: presence of sanitary toilet versus open defecation, and refuse disposal.

viva.q: What three parameters comprise the Modified Kuppuswamy socio-economic scale?
viva.a: The scale assesses the educational level of the head of the family, the occupation of the head of the family, and the total monthly family income.

viva.q: How do poor living conditions directly impact child health?
viva.a: Overcrowding accelerates respiratory infections and tuberculosis transmission, while untreated water and poor sanitation promote diarrhoea, environmental enteropathy, and parasitic infestations.

image.brief: Assessment rubric showing scoring categories of the Modified Kuppuswamy scale: parental education, head of household occupation, and family income strata.

items.summary: Structured verbal summary uniting demographic facts, presenting complaints, chronological timeline, pertinent negatives, birth, developmental, dietary, and vaccination status.

blocks.title: Standard presentation narrative format
bullets: Opening identification statement: age, sex, residence, informant identity, and assessed reliability.
Presentation timeframe: hospital setting (OPD or emergency) and duration of chief symptoms.
Synthesised timeline of presenting illness highlighting primary organ system and severity.
Concise summary of birth, past, and family history highlighting non-contributory or positive findings.
Clear declaration of developmental status, nutritional adequacy, and immunisation completeness.
Closing working hypothesis stating suspected anatomical site or clinical disease category.

blocks.title: Examiner expectations for history summary
bullets: Deliver the summary smoothly within 90 to 120 seconds without reading verbatim from notes.
Avoid repeating raw lists of negatives; highlight only diagnostic discriminators.
Accurately state whether the child was previously thriving prior to this illness.

viva.q: What essential elements must be highlighted in the opening sentence of a case summary?
viva.a: State the child's age, sex, residential origin, the primary informant and their reliability, and the acute or subacute nature of presentation to outpatient or emergency care.

viva.q: How should negative findings be presented in a clinical summary?
viva.a: Summarise negatives collectively by stating that past, perinatal, and family histories are non-contributory, mentioning only those negative features that actively exclude high-stakes differential diagnoses.

image.brief: Executive presentation outline structuring a 2-minute clinical history summary for undergraduate bedside exams.

items.summary: Systematic head-to-toe physical examination encompassing general appearance, vital signs, anthropometry, cardiorespiratory signs, craniofacial survey, and systemic clues.

blocks.title: Initial observation and general habitus
bullets: Attitude, posture of limbs, alertness, spontaneous movement, irritability, or lethargy.
Nutritional build: well-nourished, overweight, thin, wasted, or severely emaciated.
Distress indicators: tachypnoea, alar flaring, grunting, intercostal retractions, cyanosis.
Therapeutic devices: peripheral intravenous cannulae, nasogastric tubes, oxygen delivery interface.

blocks.title: Vital signs evaluation
bullets: Axillary temperature measured with a clinical thermometer, recording fever in degrees Fahrenheit.
Peripheral arterial pulse: heart rate, rhythm, volume, vessel character, radio-femoral delay, bilateral pulses.
Respiratory rate counted over one full minute, noting abdominal, abdomino-thoracic, or thoracoabdominal pattern.
Blood pressure measured using an age-appropriate cuff on the right arm in supine position.
Capillary refill time (CRT) measured on forehead or sternum, normally under 3 seconds.
Jugular venous pressure inspection for elevation, engorgement, or visible venous pulsations.

blocks.title: Anthropometric assessment
bullets: Current weight and recorded birth weight compared against age-matched standard growth percentiles.
Standing height or infant recumbent length, deriving height-for-age and weight-for-height standard deviations.
Head circumference (HC) measured along maximal occipitofrontal diameter, plotted on charts.
Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) measured at midpoint between acromion and olecranon.
Proportions: chest circumference, arm span, and upper-to-lower body segment ratio when indicated.

blocks.title: Cardiorespiratory and systemic physical signs (PICCLE)
bullets: Pallor examined on lower palpebral conjunctiva, tongue, soft palate, nail beds, and palmar creases.
Icterus inspected on upper sclera under natural daylight, soft palate, and skin.
Cyanosis evaluated on tongue and buccal mucosa (central) versus peripheral nail beds.
Clubbing assessed by looking for obliteration of Lovibond angle on digits.
Lymphadenopathy: cervical, axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal nodal enlargement, tenderness, or matted nodes.
Oedema tested by firm pressure over medial malleolus or pretibial surface for pitting.

blocks.title: Systematic cranio-caudal inspection
bullets: Skull: symmetry, shape, Macewen crack-pot sound on percussion, cranial transillumination, bruit.
Fontanelles: anterior fontanelle dimensions (normally 2.5 cm by 2.5 cm, closes by 9 to 18 months), tension, pulsatility; posterior fontanelle (normally closes by 2 months).
Facies, paranasal sinus tenderness (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid), and hair texture and colouration.
Eyes: ptosis, hypertelorism, hypotelorism, cataracts, nystagmus, strabismus, Bitot spots, xerophthalmia.
Ears, nose, throat: low-set ears, preauricular pits, cleft lip, palate, dentition, oral hygiene, tonsils.
Neck and chest: webbing, thyroid enlargement, pectus excavatum, pectus carinatum, rachitic rosary.
Skin, limbs, spine: purpura, petechiae, haemangiomas, mongolian spots, cubitus/genu deformities, scoliosis, kyphosis.

blocks.title: System-specific markers and bedside development
bullets: Neurocutaneous markers: cafe-au-lait macules, adenoma sebaceum, and ash-leaf hypopigmented macules.
Primitive and neonatal reflexes evaluated according to chronological age appropriateness.
Bedside signs of endocarditis, cardiac failure, rheumatic activity, dehydration, or hepatic dysfunction.
Bedside developmental staging across motor, social, language, visual, and auditory milestones.
Estimation of functional developmental age and bedside developmental quotient.

viva.q: What are the normal closure times for the anterior and posterior fontanelles?
viva.a: The posterior fontanelle normally closes by 2 months of age, whereas the anterior fontanelle typically closes between 9 and 18 months of age.

viva.q: What is the clinical significance of a capillary refill time exceeding 3 seconds?
viva.a: A prolonged capillary refill time indicates impaired peripheral microvascular perfusion, pointing to hypovolaemic, septic, or cardiogenic shock, or severe peripheral vasoconstriction.

viva.q: How do you distinguish central cyanosis from peripheral cyanosis?
viva.a: Central cyanosis affects warm mucosal surfaces like the tongue and oral cavity due to arterial desaturation, whereas peripheral cyanosis spares mucous membranes and reflects sluggish capillary blood flow.

image.brief: Full-body anatomical diagram showing the paediatric head-to-toe examination sequence from fontanelle inspection to peripheral pulse palpation.

items.summary: Structured examination of individual organ systems including cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, central nervous, and musculoskeletal systems.

blocks.title: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination
bullets: Cardiovascular system: inspection of precordium, apex beat localisation, thrills, heart sounds, murmurs.
Respiratory system: chest wall symmetry, respiratory rate, trachea position, percussion note, breath sounds, adventitious crepitations or wheezes.

blocks.title: Abdominal and nervous system examination
bullets: Gastrointestinal and abdominal examination: abdominal distension, superficial veins, liver and spleen palpation, fluid thrill, bowel sounds.
Central nervous system: cranial nerve assessment, motor tone, muscle power, deep tendon reflexes, clonus, plantar response, sensory examination.
Musculoskeletal system: spinal alignment, joint range of motion, swelling, warmth, joint effusion.

viva.q: In what order should systemic examination be performed in an uncooperative toddler?
viva.a: Perform opportunistic auscultation of heart and lungs first while the child is quiet or sleeping, leaving distressing or intrusive maneuvers like throat and abdominal palpation for the end.

viva.q: How does the normal site of the apex beat vary with age in childhood?
viva.a: In infants and young children under 4 years, the apex beat lies in the 4th intercostal space lateral to the midclavicular line; by age 7, it shifts to the 5th intercostal space within the midclavicular line.

image.brief: Five-system clinical overview diagram detailing chest, precordium, abdominal quadrants, cranial nerves, and musculoskeletal joints.

title.en: Synthesised examination and comprehensive case summary

items.summary: Unified clinical summary integrating key historical data and salient physical findings into an evidence-based clinical presentation.

blocks.title: Core components of the final summary
bullets: State child demographic details, chief complaints, and duration of current illness.
Summarise key positive physical findings across general and systemic examination.
Integrate pertinent negative signs that rule out critical complications or differential diagnoses.
Explicitly state nutritional status, developmental quotient, and immunisation status for age.
Conclude with an overarching clinical diagnostic impression.

blocks.title: Examiner evaluation standards
bullets: Demonstrates clinical synthesis rather than repeating individual organ-system lists.
Correlates systemic examination findings directly with the initial history.
Highlights the presence or absence of decompensation, shock, or respiratory failure.

viva.q: What distinguishes an outstanding case summary in a clinical examination?
viva.a: An outstanding summary seamlessly connects the historical chronology with key physical findings, integrates nutritional and developmental status, and justifies the working diagnosis logically.

viva.q: Why must nutritional and developmental status be explicitly stated in the summary?
viva.a: Nutritional and developmental health represent the overall resilience of the paediatric patient, dictate prognosis, and directly modify drug selection and supportive management plans.

image.brief: Structured summary synthesis framework balancing history chronology, key physical signs, nutritional status, and diagnostic impression.

items.summary: Comprehensive multi-axial diagnostic formulation specifying anatomical involvement, physiological derangement, suspected aetiology, severity, and nutritional-developmental status.

blocks.title: Multi-axial diagnostic components
bullets: Anatomical diagnosis: precise tissue, organ, or anatomical compartment affected.
Physiological and pathological diagnosis: functional consequence such as congestive failure, bronchospasm, or raised intracranial pressure.
Aetiological diagnosis: presumed underlying infectious, congenital, autoimmune, or metabolic cause.
Severity and acuity: acute, subacute, or chronic presentation, with staging or risk stratification.
Comorbid status: nutritional grading (PEM status), developmental status, and immunisation completion.

blocks.title: Example of complete diagnosis structure
bullets: Formulate as: A known chronological age child presenting with acute primary disorder, complicated by secondary physiology, in a background of defined nutritional status.
Avoid one-word generic diagnoses like pneumonia or fever; specify lobe, severity, and complications.

viva.q: Why is a single-word diagnosis unacceptable in a paediatric clinical exam?
viva.a: A complete paediatric diagnosis must encompass anatomical site, functional derangement, presumed aetiology, acute severity, complications, and underlying nutritional and developmental comorbidities.

viva.q: How does patient age influence the presumed aetiology in a provisional diagnosis?
viva.a: Pathogen epidemiology and disease vulnerability change dramatically across neonatal, infantile, toddler, and school-age groups, directing age-specific aetiological reasoning.

image.brief: Multi-axial diagnosis schema showing blocks for anatomy, physiology, aetiology, acute severity, and nutritional developmental modifiers.

items.summary: Structured prioritisation of alternative clinical conditions sharing symptoms and signs, defended with specific positive and negative clinical discriminators.

blocks.title: Structuring differential diagnoses
bullets: List two to three plausible alternative diagnoses in order of decreasing likelihood.
Base each candidate diagnosis on specific historical clues, age profile, and physical signs.
Explicitly state points in favour of each differential from the patient findings.
Explicitly state points against each differential that make it less likely than the provisional diagnosis.

blocks.title: Common diagnostic dilemmas
bullets: Wheezing infant: viral bronchiolitis versus reactive airway disease versus foreign body aspiration.
Acute febrile encephalopathy: bacterial meningitis versus viral meningoencephalitis versus cerebral malaria.
Abdominal pain with vomiting: acute appendicitis versus mesenteric adenitis versus intussusception.

viva.q: How should a candidate defend their primary diagnosis against a close differential?
viva.a: Compare both entities directly, highlighting pathognomonic physical signs, disease progression, and atypical features that favour the primary diagnosis while explaining why the alternative is less probable.

viva.q: What rule must govern the selection of differential diagnoses in an examination?
viva.a: Differentials must be clinically plausible and common for the patient's age and presentation; rare syndromes should not be offered ahead of common paediatric pathologies.

image.brief: Decision tree diagram comparing candidate clinical differentials against points in favour and points against for paediatric case discussions.

items.summary: Stepwise diagnostic strategy detailing bedside tests, baseline laboratory investigations, imaging modalities, and confirmatory microbiological or genetic assays.

blocks.title: Tiered investigation framework
bullets: Bedside and point-of-care testing: blood glucose, pulse oximetry, urine dipstick, rapid malarial test.
Baseline haematology and biochemistry: complete blood count, peripheral smear, renal and liver function panels, serum electrolytes.
Microbiological work-up: blood culture, urine microscopy and culture, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, sputum or gastric aspirate.
Diagnostic imaging: plain radiography (chest, abdomen), ultrasonography, echocardiography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging.

blocks.title: Principles of rational test ordering
bullets: Justify every requested test by how its result alters immediate clinical decision-making.
Prioritise non-invasive and emergency resuscitation diagnostics before scheduling invasive tests.
Sequence tests logically: emergency stabilization panels first, followed by definitive confirmatory testing.

viva.q: What immediate bedside tests must be requested before sending formal blood panels?
viva.a: Point-of-care blood glucose must be tested immediately to detect life-threatening hypoglycaemia, alongside continuous pulse oximetry for hypoxaemia and a urine dipstick if indicated.

viva.q: Why must blood cultures be drawn prior to starting parenteral antimicrobials?
viva.a: Administering antibiotics before blood collection rapidly clears circulating bacteraemia, preventing organism isolation, identification, and antimicrobial sensitivity profiling.

image.brief: Tiered diagnostic testing pyramid showing bedside point-of-care tests at the base, routine biochemistry in the middle, and advanced imaging at the apex.

title.en: Stepwise paediatric management and treatment plan

items.summary: Holistic treatment framework spanning emergency triage, airway-breathing-circulation stabilization, fluid management, disease-specific therapy, and supportive nursing.

blocks.title: Emergency triage and supportive stabilization
bullets: Airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) triage and emergency resuscitation.
Oxygen therapy delivered via nasal prongs, face mask, or high-flow nasal cannula.
Intravenous fluid resuscitation in shock (isotonic crystalloid boluses) followed by maintenance fluids.
Thermal control, correction of hypoglycaemia, and continuous vital signs monitoring.

blocks.title: Targeted and definitive medical therapy
bullets: Disease-specific pharmacotherapy: empiric parenteral antimicrobials, bronchodilators, anticonvulsants.
Accurate drug dose calculation based on body weight in kilograms, checking renal adjustments.
Nutritional support: continued breastfeeding, enteral feeding via nasogastric tube, or parenteral nutrition.
Supportive nursing care: position changes, skin care, fluid balance charting, and pain relief.

viva.q: What is the initial fluid bolus recommendation for a child in hypovolaemic shock?
viva.a: Administer 20 ml per kg of an isotonic crystalloid, such as Ringer lactate or 0.9 percent normal saline, rapidly over 10 to 20 minutes, reassessing vitals and perfusion immediately.

viva.q: Why is weight-based dosing mandatory for all paediatric pharmacotherapy?
viva.a: Children exhibit marked age-related pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic variations; adult dosing schedules cause severe toxicity or therapeutic failure, requiring precise milligram per kilogram dosing.

title.en: Preventive paediatrics, parental counselling, and follow-up

items.summary: Secondary and tertiary preventive interventions including catch-up immunisation, nutritional counselling, family screening, developmental stimulation, and follow-up.

blocks.title: Preventive interventions and counselling
bullets: Catch-up immunisation audit to administer any missed national schedule or optional vaccines.
Nutritional counselling emphasizing exclusive breastfeeding, diverse complementary feeding, and micronutrients.
Environmental health guidance: safe drinking water, hand hygiene, avoidance of indoor biomass smoke.
Screening family members and contacts for infectious diseases such as tuberculosis.

blocks.title: Discharge planning and surveillance
bullets: Parental education regarding red flag warning signs requiring immediate return to emergency care.
Scheduled follow-up visits to monitor somatic growth, developmental milestones, and organ recovery.
Referral to early developmental intervention services or subspecialist clinics when indicated.

viva.q: What parental danger signs necessitate urgent hospital return following discharge?
viva.a: Caregivers must seek immediate care if the child develops inability to feed, persistent vomiting, lethargy or reduced consciousness, convulsions, rapid breathing, or cold extremities.

viva.q: How does primary prevention in paediatrics reduce long-term morbidity?
viva.a: Timely vaccination prevents fatal infectious diseases, optimal infant nutrition prevents stunting and micronutrient deficiencies, and environmental sanitation interrupts the enteric pathogen cycle.
